prompt: "Why should we believe this forensic chemist's testimony on the toxic runoff when she was divorced twice and declared personal bankruptcy last year?"
mechanism: Attacking the personal character, background, or circumstances of the claimant rather than analyzing the empirical validity of their argument.
countermeasure: Decouple the claimant's character from the claim's logic: 'Even if her personal finances are disordered, is her chemical chromatography data objectively accurate?'

prompt: A luxury watch is displayed next to a sign reading 'MSRP $12,000 — Today Only $1,800', making buyers perceive $1,800 as an unbeatable bargain despite the watch costing $40 to manufacture.
mechanism: Disproportionately weighting the first piece of numerical information encountered (the 'anchor') when making subsequent quantitative assessments.
countermeasure: Independent baseline valuation: Research wholesale manufacturing costs and competitive market prices before evaluating discounts.

prompt: "Arsenic and botulinum toxin are 100% natural compounds found in the earth, whereas penicillin is synthetically cultured in laboratories. Therefore, arsenic is healthier for human consumption than penicillin."
mechanism: Equating 'natural' with 'good, safe, and wholesome', and 'synthetic' with 'bad, toxic, and dangerous'.
countermeasure: Point to biological toxins: Nature produces cyanide and ricin; safety is determined by molecular pharmacology, not origin.

prompt: Name the move: ""A commercial PR firm deploys 5,000 bot accounts to coordinate posts praising a new luxury car model, making it appear like a genuine grassroots viral trend.""
mechanism: Not: Bandwagon Effect, Card Stacking, Loaded Language
countermeasure: Orchestrating an artificial marketing campaign masked as spontaneous, grassroots citizen consensus.

prompt: Name the move: "Six months before any content appears, an operator buys expired domains whose names resemble regional newspapers and lets them sit dormant."
mechanism: Not: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution, T0001: Target Profiling, Brigading
countermeasure: Asset creation and ageing happen in the Prepare phase, long before anything is seeded — dormancy is the point, since domain age is a trust signal. Target profiling is the neighbouring Plan-phase activity and would involve studying an audience rather than building infrastructure.

prompt: Name the move: "An adversary scrapes a year of a community's public posts to identify its most-shared grievances and the ten accounts everyone replies to."
mechanism: Not: T0004: Establish Inauthentic Assets / Spoofing, T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution, Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour
countermeasure: Audience research precedes narrative development: you need to know which grievance exists before you can amplify it. Nothing has been created or published yet, which is what places this in Plan rather than Prepare.

prompt: Name the move: "A team drafts three variants of a narrative and quietly tests each with small ad buys to see which produces the most engagement, before any organic push."
mechanism: Not: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution, T0001: Target Profiling, Astroturfing
countermeasure: This is message optimisation inside the Prepare phase — the same A/B discipline commercial marketing uses. It follows target profiling and precedes seeding, and its signature is small, cheap, low-visibility activity that looks like nothing much at the time.

prompt: Name the move: "Personas are built with two years of backdated ordinary posts — recipes, sport, holiday photographs — before ever mentioning politics."
mechanism: Not: Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour, T0001: Target Profiling, Astroturfing
countermeasure: Legend-building is asset preparation; the mundane history exists to defeat exactly the account-age and content-mix checks a reviewer would run. It becomes a deployed astroturf campaign only once those assets are used to simulate a movement.

prompt: Name the move: "A fabricated claim is posted first to a small niche forum, then screenshotted into a mid-size channel as "people are saying", then covered by a national outlet as a controversy."
mechanism: Not: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution, Astroturfing, Firehose of Falsehood
countermeasure: Each hop strips provenance and adds apparent credibility until the origin is unrecoverable. Flooding is a different mechanism — volume rather than laundering — and the tell here is the deliberate ladder of venues.

prompt: Name the move: "Prepared assets post a claim simultaneously across six platforms within a four-minute window."
mechanism: Not: T0004: Establish Inauthentic Assets / Spoofing, Brigading, T0001: Target Profiling
countermeasure: Simultaneity across platforms is the seeding signature — it manufactures the appearance of independent emergence, which is the single strongest trust cue an audience has. Brigading would target one venue or account rather than spreading across many.

prompt: Name the move: "Operators identify accounts that already believe a related claim and supply them with polished graphics, then step back entirely."
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing, Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour, Brigading
countermeasure: The amplifiers are entirely authentic, which is what makes this so hard to counter — there is no inauthentic network to take down, and the sincerity of the spreaders is real. Astroturfing requires manufactured participants; this recruits genuine ones.

prompt: Name the move: "A campaign seeds a hashtag at 03:00 local time, when moderation staffing is thinnest, and lets it trend before review."
mechanism: Not: Brigading, T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution, Cross-Platform Amplification
countermeasure: Trending status acquired before human review converts into organic reach that survives the later takedown. The operational insight is that platform defences have a schedule, and schedules are targetable.

prompt: Name the move: "Thousands of low-quality posts on an unrelated topic bury a damaging story in every relevant feed within hours."
diagnosis: T0048: Flood the Information Environment / Epistemic Pollution
mechanism: Not: Narrative Laundering, Gish Gallop, Brigading
countermeasure: Nothing is argued and nothing is denied — attention is simply displaced. A Gish gallop floods a DEBATE with claims; this floods a channel with noise, and needs no engagement with the story at all.

prompt: Name the move: ""An image of a politician shows perfectly circular pupils, but the light reflections in the left and right eyes depict completely different room window angles and shapes.""
mechanism: Not: Error Level Analysis Inconsistency, Frequency Domain Smearing, GAN Border Ringing
countermeasure: Diffusion generators render each eye independently, frequently failing physics-based specular ray alignment.

prompt: Name the move: "A small false claim is circulating in one niche forum. An agency issues a national press release naming and rebutting it."
diagnosis: The countermeasure amplifies what it targets
mechanism: Not: Prebunking, Strategic Silence (Deliberate Non-Amplification), Narrative Laundering
countermeasure: The rebuttal carries the claim to an audience that had never encountered it, and repetition increases familiarity, which increases believability. Proportionality is the whole skill — the right response to a contained claim is often containment.

prompt: Name the move: "Before an expected influence operation, an outlet explains the TECHNIQUE likely to be used, without repeating any specific false claim."
mechanism: Not: Debunking, Strategic Silence (Deliberate Non-Amplification), Counter-Messaging
countermeasure: Teaching the manipulation pattern in advance confers resistance without giving the specific falsehood any airtime. That is its advantage over debunking, which necessarily repeats the claim in order to correct it.

prompt: Name the move: "An image carries a C2PA manifest that parses cleanly. The viewer shows the capture device, edit history and signer."
diagnosis: The manifest is parsed but not cryptographically verified
mechanism: Not: The image is proven authentic, The image is proven edited, The manifest proves the device model
countermeasure: Parsing reads what a file claims about itself; verification requires checking the COSE signature against a trusted certificate chain and confirming the asset hashes still match. A well-formed manifest can be copied wholesale onto a different image.

prompt: Name the move: "A photograph has no C2PA manifest at all."
diagnosis: This is not evidence of tampering
mechanism: Not: This indicates the image was manipulated, This indicates the image is synthetic, This proves the metadata was stripped deliberately
countermeasure: The overwhelming majority of images ever made carry no manifest, and ordinary pipelines — screenshots, messaging apps, re-encodes — strip them routinely. Treating absence as suspicion would flag almost every real photograph in existence.

prompt: Name the move: "A manifest verifies cryptographically. The signing certificate chains to a certificate authority the analyst has never heard of."
diagnosis: The signature is valid but says nothing about the signer's trustworthiness
mechanism: Not: The image is authentic, The signature is invalid, The image was captured by the named device
countermeasure: Cryptography establishes that a particular key signed particular bytes; whether that key belongs to anyone worth believing is a trust decision outside the mathematics. Anyone can stand up a CA and sign their own fabrications perfectly.

prompt: Name the move: "A manifest records that the asset was generated by a text-to-image model, and the signature verifies."
diagnosis: Strong evidence the image is synthetic, since a generator had no incentive to lie
mechanism: Not: Proof the image is synthetic, No information — manifests can be forged, Evidence the image is authentic
countermeasure: A self-declared disclosure signed by the tool that made it is credible in the direction that costs the declarer something. Note the asymmetry: a manifest claiming CAMERA capture is far weaker evidence, because that is the claim an adversary would want to make.

prompt: Name the move: "Two copies of an image circulate. One carries a valid manifest; the other is pixel-identical with the manifest stripped."
diagnosis: Stripping a manifest is trivial and leaves the pixels untouched
mechanism: Not: The stripped copy has been manipulated, The manifest copy must be the original, The two files cannot be pixel-identical
countermeasure: Provenance is carried alongside the image data, not embedded in it, so removal changes nothing visible. This is why C2PA can raise confidence when present and can never lower it when absent.

prompt: Name the move: "An Error Level Analysis view shows one region markedly brighter than the rest of the frame."
diagnosis: An indicator with several innocent explanations, not a finding
mechanism: Not: Proof that region was pasted in, Proof the image is synthetic, Evidence the image is unedited
countermeasure: Differing JPEG compression history produces the same signature — a crop, a resave, text overlay, or a region of genuinely different texture will all light up. ELA locates something worth asking about; it does not answer the question.

prompt: Name the move: "A hiring panel that liked a candidate's first answer spends the rest of the interview asking questions the candidate is likely to answer well."
mechanism: Not: Anchoring Effect, Fundamental Attribution Error / Ingroup Favoritism, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: The interview stops being a test once the questions are chosen to be passed. Anchoring is a defensible second answer — the first answer did set an impression — but the diagnostic feature here is that the panel is now GATHERING evidence selectively rather than merely weighting it.

prompt: Name the move: ""A suspected leaked audio file features an official's voice with zero audible inhalation pauses across 90 seconds of uninterrupted rapid speech.""
mechanism: Not: Frequency Cutoff Artifact, Phase Cancellation, Vocal Fry Modulation
countermeasure: Text-to-speech (TTS) neural models stitch phonemes together without natural biological breathing rhythms or nasal friction.

prompt: Name the move: ""Inspecting a crowd photograph reveals that distant spectators' earlobes blend seamlessly into their collars, and glasses frames fade into cheek skin without hinges.""
mechanism: Not: Chroma Subsampling, JPEG Block Boundary Artifact, Sensor Bayer Filter Pattern
countermeasure: Generative diffusion models struggle with fine semantic topological continuity around complex accessory boundaries.

prompt: Name the move: ""An adversary state maps existing ethnic and socio-economic tension points across social media groups months before launching an influence operation.""
mechanism: Not: T0016: Synthetic Media Creation, T0035: Botnet Swarming, T0047: Media Infiltration
countermeasure: DISARM Tactic T0001 (Target Profiling) operates in the planning stage to identify societal fault lines for weaponized exploitation.

prompt: Name the move: "A friend sends you a video captioned "They don't want you to see this!" Your hands are already typing a reply. What is the SIFT-correct first move?"
diagnosis: Pause and notice the urgency pull before doing anything else
mechanism: Not: Forward it to a group chat and ask whether anyone there thinks it looks fake, Watch the video again frame by frame for editing artifacts, Quote-tweet it with a question mark to test the reaction
countermeasure: STOP is the first SIFT move: noticing the emotional hook and pausing precedes every investigation step. Sharing to test reactions amplifies the claim; frame analysis skips the pause.

prompt: Name the move: "A post makes your blood boil and the share button feels urgent. According to SIFT, why is the pause itself the step that most determines what happens next?"
diagnosis: Sharing is largely irreversible, and investigation only happens if you haven't already amplified
mechanism: Not: Anger impairs your ability to read captions accurately, Pausing briefly lets the platform's community fact-check label appear on the post before you decide, Posts shared in anger are permanently demoted by algorithms
countermeasure: SIFT treats Stop as pivotal because amplification is the harm: once shared, the claim travels regardless of later correction. The other options invent platform behaviors or misread the skill.

prompt: Name the move: "You feel a strong urge to repost a alarming statistic about crime rising in your city. Which action best fulfills the SIFT Stop step rather than a later step?"
diagnosis: Naming the emotion the claim triggered and deciding not to act on it yet
mechanism: Not: Searching the city's open crime data portal immediately for the statistic being cited, Checking who first published the statistic, Looking for a second news outlet reporting the same number
countermeasure: Stop is the metacognitive moment: recognizing the emotional pull and declining to act on it immediately. The other three are Investigate the Source, Find, and Trace — later steps.

prompt: Name the move: "A claim arrives in a slick newsletter you have never heard of, "The Civic Ledger." Which SIFT step applies, and what does it actually require?"
diagnosis: Investigate the Source: establish what the outlet is, who funds it, and its track record
mechanism: Not: Investigate the Source: read the newsletter's own About page and accept what it says, Stop: refuse to read any newsletter you have never heard of, Find Better Coverage: locate two other outlets citing The Civic Ledger, which would show its reach if not its accuracy
countermeasure: Investigate the Source means independent knowledge of the source — funding, track record, reputation — not trusting its self-description. Reading the About page is the classic failure mode.

prompt: Name the move: "Before evaluating an exposé from "Health Freedom Daily," which question belongs to SIFT's Investigate step?"
diagnosis: Who funds this outlet and what has it published that checked out or didn't?
mechanism: Not: Is the exposé's central claim emotionally persuasive enough that readers will finish it?, How many shares and comments does the exposé have?, Does the exposé cite an official-sounding agency?
countermeasure: SIFT's source investigation is about funding and track record — provenance and reliability. Popularity, emotional pull, and official-sounding citations are exactly the cues the step tells you to look past.

prompt: Name the move: "An anonymous account breaks a story about a competitor company. Which combination best completes the SIFT Investigate step?"
diagnosis: The account's history, its funding or affiliation, and its record on past claims
mechanism: Not: The story's plausibility and whether the account has many followers and high engagement, Whether the company denies it and how quickly, Whether the story uses confident, specific language
countermeasure: SIFT asks what the source is — history, incentives, track record — before the claim is engaged. Follower counts, denial speed, and confident prose are surface cues, not reliability evidence.

prompt: Name the move: "A video's caption insists a doctor said vaccines cause autism. What is SIFT's Find Better Coverage move here?"
diagnosis: Open new tabs and see what health agencies and independent outlets say about the claim
mechanism: Not: Watch several more videos from the same channel to check whether its claims are internally consistent, Read the video's description for cited papers, Ask the uploader for their sources in the comments
countermeasure: Find Better Coverage is lateral reading: leave the page, consult better-placed sources on the same claim. Staying within the uploader's ecosystem or their own citations is vertical reading.

prompt: Name the move: "You find one obscure blog claiming a city banned gasoline cars overnight. Which behavior is the SIFT Find step, correctly done?"
diagnosis: Searching whether any reliable outlet or the city itself reports such a decision
mechanism: Not: Reading the blog's full argument carefully from start to finish before judging it, Checking whether the blog allows comments, Searching for other people who shared the blog's claim
countermeasure: The move is toward better-placed coverage: does the city say this, do reliable outlets? Reading deeper into the source, engagement metrics, and echo prevalence are all failures of the step.

prompt: Name the move: "A dramatic screenshot of a news headline is circulating. What does the SIFT Find Better Coverage step say about the screenshot itself?"
diagnosis: Leave the screenshot: search for the story and see how other sources report it
mechanism: Not: Zoom in closely to check whether the headline font matches the outlet's usual typography, Reverse-image search the screenshot to find its first posting, Reply to the sharer asking where they got it
countermeasure: Find means consulting independent coverage of the underlying story, not forensic work on the artifact. Font inspection and reverse-image search are useful but belong to other verification toolkits, not this step.

prompt: Name the move: "A politician is quoted saying something shocking. Before reacting, what does SIFT's Trace step require?"
diagnosis: Finding the original speech or transcript and checking what changed between it and the quote
mechanism: Not: Checking the politician's party affiliation, voting record, and history of controversial statements, Finding how many outlets repeated the quote, Asking a fact-checker whether the politician is generally trustworthy
countermeasure: Trace follows the claim upstream to its original context and notes mutations en route. Track record and repetition volume are context, not the trace itself.

prompt: Name the move: "A statistic travels with the caption "crime doubled under the current mayor." What is the SIFT Trace move for this number?"
diagnosis: Locate the original dataset or report and compare its actual finding to the caption
mechanism: Not: Search for other posts using the same caption to see how widely it has already traveled, Check whether the poster has shared crime stories before, Find a criminologist's general opinion of crime statistics
countermeasure: Tracing means reaching the primary source — the dataset or report — and diffing what it says against what the caption says. Echoes, poster history, and generic expert opinion do not recover the original context.

prompt: Name the move: "An image of a flooded street is captioned as being from this week's storm. Which sequence is the SIFT Trace step done thoroughly?"
diagnosis: Reverse-image search to the earliest appearance, then establish the original date, place, and event
mechanism: Not: Check the image's resolution and whether it looks like it was shot by a professional photographer on scene, Look for other flooded-street images from this week to compare, Ask the original poster when they took the photo
countermeasure: Tracing an image means finding its earliest publication and recovering original context — date, place, event — and noticing what the recaption changed. Image quality and comparison sets are not the trace.

prompt: Name the move: ""The policy must be working — after all, the reason it works is that policies like it always succeed.""
mechanism: Not: Post hoc reasoning, Appeal to Authority (Argumentum ad Verecundiam), Red herring
countermeasure: The conclusion (it works) is smuggled into the premise (policies like it always succeed) — the argument goes nowhere except in a circle. That is question-begging, a structural defect, not a distraction or a causal error.

prompt: Name the move: ""Since the city started spraying organic mosquito repellent in July, local bakery sales have doubled. Clearly, mosquito repellent stimulates carbohydrate appetite.""
mechanism: Not: Genetic Fallacy, Circular Reasoning (Petitio Principii), Equivocation
countermeasure: Confuses chronological sequence with causal relationship ('after this, therefore because of this').

prompt: Name the move: "Survey: "Have you stopped ignoring the safety reports your department filed?" — an inspector demands an answer as proof of negligence."
mechanism: Not: Hasty generalisation, Straw man, Appeal to tradition
countermeasure: The question presupposes the conclusion (that reports were ignored) inside its phrasing, so any direct answer concedes it. This loaded structure is the classic complex question.

prompt: Name the move: ""If the new thermostat is installed, energy bills will drop. Bills dropped last quarter, so the new thermostat must be installed.""
mechanism: Not: Denying the Antecedent (Inverse Error), Slippery slope, Texas sharpshooter
countermeasure: The form is: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Observing the consequent (bills dropped) does not license the antecedent (thermostat installed) — warm weather could also lower bills. This is affirming the consequent, a formal fallacy.

prompt: Name the move: ""Of course Senator Ortega's tax study is wrong — she wrote it while under investigation, so nothing she touches can be trusted.""
mechanism: Not: Genetic fallacy only in origin, not circumstantial, Tu quoque, False balance
countermeasure: The study is dismissed via the author's situation rather than its data or method — the circumstantial ad hominem. Tu quoque would require pointing at her own hypocrisy; the genetic fallacy label alone misses the circumstantial mechanism the skill targets.

prompt: Name the move: ""How can you lecture anyone about recycling when you flew to a conference last year?""
mechanism: Not: Straw man, Red herring, Composition
countermeasure: The argument dismisses the recycling case by pointing at the arguer's own inconsistent behavior — you do it too. That is tu quoque: a relevance fallacy that substitutes the arguer's conduct for the argument.

prompt: Name the move: ""My grandfather smoked a pack a day and lived to 94, so the scare studies are overblown.""
mechanism: Not: Survivorship bias as a separate mechanism from anecdote, Base-rate neglect, Appeal to tradition
countermeasure: A single personal case is offered against aggregate evidence — the anecdotal-evidence fallacy, a scope error. Survivorship and base-rate are related biases, but the argument's surface move is the one-case-against-many substitution.

prompt: Name the move: ""Every park in the city that installed new lights saw fewer complaints afterwards — so new lights cut complaints.""
mechanism: Not: Hasty generalisation, Texas sharpshooter, Division
countermeasure: Sequence is read as causation: lights first, fewer complaints after, therefore lights caused it. With no control for other changes, this is post hoc. The sample is citywide, so it is neither small nor cherry-picked from a larger pool.

prompt: Name the move: ""Dr. Lin, who led the WHO's air-quality panel, says the standard is outdated. But Dr. Boone, a sports physiologist, disagrees — so the evidence is split.""
mechanism: Not: False balance, Hasty generalisation, Genetic fallacy
countermeasure: The weight is manufactured by parading a speaker without relevant expertise as a counterweight — false authority. False balance describes news framing of a two-sided debate; here the specific defect is the substituted credential.

prompt: Name the move: ""No one has ever proved these supplements are harmful, so I'll keep recommending them to patients.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to authority, Base-rate neglect, Begging the question
countermeasure: Absence of disproof is treated as proof of safety — the appeal to ignorance. The claim's advocate even wears an authority role, but the inferential defect is the absence-to-conclusion move.

prompt: Name the move: ""The CEO's health plan must be flawless because our company employs 100,000 highly intelligent engineers who all endorse it enthusiastically.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Pity, Affirming the Consequent, False Analogy
countermeasure: Asserts a claim is true or optimal solely because a large multitude of people endorse it.

prompt: Name the move: "After reading three articles about shark attacks, a swimmer rates shark attacks as a top-five cause of accidental death. What bias does this illustrate?"
diagnosis: Availability — judging frequency by ease of recall
mechanism: Not: Anchoring — clinging to the first number seen and under-adjusting from it afterwards, Confirmation bias — seeking supportive evidence, Hindsight bias — rewriting what was knowable
countermeasure: Recent, vivid coverage makes shark attacks easy to bring to mind, and ease of recall is mistaken for frequency — the availability mechanism that high-volume coverage exploits.

prompt: Name the move: "A negotiator opens at $1,000 for a used laptop worth about $600, and the buyer feels $780 is a win. What bias shaped the buyer's judgment?"
mechanism: Not: Availability of cheap laptops, Confirmation bias about laptop value, Sunk-cost fallacy
countermeasure: The first number in the negotiation disproportionally constrains the range the buyer considers reasonable — the anchoring effect, including how a stated frame constrains the answers considered.

prompt: Name the move: "A manager reads a study that vitamin D helps sleep, then bookmarks only the supportive studies and skims past two rigorous null results. What is this pattern?"
diagnosis: Confirmation bias in evidence selection and interpretation
mechanism: Not: Availability bias from recent reading, Attribution error — explaining the study authors' null results by their carelessness, Base-rate neglect
countermeasure: Selective search and selective interpretation of evidence to fit a prior belief is confirmation bias — here operating in the manager's own research behavior, which the skill explicitly covers.

prompt: Name the move: "A colleague misses a deadline and you call him careless; you miss one the same week and explain the client kept changing the brief. What is this asymmetry?"
mechanism: Not: Self-serving attribution as a distinct mechanism, Ingroup favouritism, Hindsight bias
countermeasure: Others' behavior is explained by disposition (careless), your own by circumstance (client changes) — the classic fundamental attribution error the skill names. The skill covers both halves; the pairing is its signature pattern.

prompt: Name the move: "A startup has spent $2M building a product the market rejected. The board votes to spend $1M more to "finish what we started" rather than pivot. What error drives the vote?"
mechanism: Not: Anchoring on the $2M figure, Base-rate neglect, Overconfidence bias
countermeasure: Past expenditure, unrecoverable either way, is used to justify further investment — the sunk-cost error the skill names. Anchoring would require the $2M to distort a numeric judgment; here it is the commitment logic that is defective.

prompt: Name the move: "400 accounts created in the same week, all posting near-identical praise for a mayoral candidate, all listing the same out-of-state gym. What is this?"
mechanism: Not: Organic grassroots support, Flooding the thread with copypasta and repeated slogans, Seed-stage information operation, pre-viral
countermeasure: Manufactured grassroots appearance — creation clustering, near-identical phrasing, shared off-topic identity markers — is the astroturfing signature the skill trains. The campaign is already visible, so 'pre-viral' misreads it.

prompt: Name the move: "A product's reviews surge overnight: dozens of five-star posts, each thanking "the team at Driftwell" in the same sentence structure, several from accounts whose only other activity is a different brand's review posted minutes earlier. What tactic is most strongly indicated?"
mechanism: Not: Genuine word-of-mouth after a marketing push, Flooding of the review channel to bury the few critical reviews, Equivocation in the product's claims
countermeasure: Creation and posting synchrony plus templated phrasing plus reused accounts across brands is the manufactured-grassroots pattern — inauthentic coordination dressed as customers. Flooding targets channels with volume; no semantic shift is present.

prompt: Name the move: "In a comment thread, one side posts forty links in ten minutes, each with a one-line slogan. Replies citing sources are buried. What tactic is this?"
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing the thread, False balance between the two sides of the thread, Loaded language
countermeasure: The goal is not persuasion by any single argument but overwhelming the channel so refutation cost exceeds assertion cost and signal is buried — flooding, with Gish-gallop rhythm at thread scale.

prompt: Name the move: "A segment on vaccine safety gives a virologist two minutes and a wellness influencer two minutes, framing the science as "the debate continues." What tactic is this?"
diagnosis: False balance — presenting asymmetric evidence as a two-sided debate
mechanism: Not: Flooding the segment with voices, Astroturfing the audience with planted questioners and paid on-air reactions, Equivocation on 'science'
countermeasure: Equal airtime for unequal expertise manufactures doubt by making consensus look contested — false balance, exactly the 'both sides' misrepresentation the skill targets. The segment is not flooding (few voices) nor semantic shift.

prompt: Name the move: ""The regime's thugs shattered the peaceful protest," versus "Officers responded to the unruly mob." Same event. What device is at work?"
mechanism: Not: False balance between the two competing narratives of the event, Equivocation on 'protest', Flooding with adjectives
countermeasure: Each description's word choice (thugs/shattered vs unruly/mob) imports a verdict about who is legitimate — emotive framing doing the argument's work before any evidence is offered.

prompt: Name the move: "A fundraiser's page reads: "Every hour you hesitate, another family loses their home. Will you stand with families — or look away?" What is the framing doing?"
diagnosis: Constraining the choice set so declining feels like harming families
mechanism: Not: False balance between the option of donating and the option of not donating, Astroturfing urgency, Equivocation on 'family'
countermeasure: The question's wording makes one response feel like the only decent one — framing that fuses donating with decency and anything else with looking away. That is the loaded-frame mechanism, not balance, coordination, or semantic shift.

prompt: Name the move: ""Expensive energy is bad for families. This subsidy keeps energy cheap. Therefore the subsidy is good for families." Midway, 'cheap' shifts from low prices to low-quality supply. What is this failure?"
diagnosis: Equivocation — a term changing meaning across the argument
mechanism: Not: Begging the Question (Petitio Principii) on the subsidy's value, False balance, Composition
countermeasure: The conclusion trades on 'cheap' meaning low-price in the premises and degraded-quality in the conclusion — a semantic shift the argument depends on, the definition of equivocation.

prompt: Name the move: "Analysts notice a new network of social accounts researching local election officials, building follower bases with benign pet content, and registering near-identical domain names. No influence content has been posted. Which DISARM stage fits?"
diagnosis: Plan and Prepare — target profiling and asset establishment
mechanism: Not: Seed — the accounts are seeding benign content, Amplify — the benign pet content is already being amplified across platforms, Measure Effectiveness — the follower count is the effect
countermeasure: Target profiling, narrative development, and asset establishment before visible influence content are Plan/Prepare activity. Benign pet content is asset-building, not seeding of the influence narrative; nothing has been amplified yet.

prompt: Name the move: "A dormant network of 60 accounts suddenly publishes a shared narrative document across four platforms within two hours, each account posting a customized variant. Which DISARM TTPs are most directly indicated?"
diagnosis: Seed and Amplify — cross-platform seeding with synchronised variants
mechanism: Not: Plan and Prepare — document drafting is preparation, Countermeasure — the customized variants show adaptive response to earlier takedowns, Measure — the two-hour window is the measured effect
countermeasure: Placing the narrative into the environment through inauthentic assets and spreading it across platforms is Seed plus Amplify. Preparation happened earlier; the variants are deployment, not adaptation to response.

prompt: Name the move: "A platform deletes 200 coordinated accounts, and the operator's next move is a post claiming "they're censoring the truth — see for yourself." What did the countermeasure risk doing?"
diagnosis: Amplifying the narrative by feeding a censorship story
mechanism: Not: Failing to measure the campaign's reach before and after the takedown, Misclassifying Seed activity as Amplify, Nothing — takedowns carry no downside
countermeasure: Visible takedowns can be converted into evidence of suppression, amplifying the very narrative they targeted — the proportionality and blowback awareness the countermeasure skill trains.

prompt: Name the move: "A hoax about water contamination is circulating in one town, still small and local. Officials are deciding between a loud public rebuttal, quiet correction via local trusted channels, and platform reporting. Which choice is most proportionate to the stage?"
diagnosis: Quiet correction through local trusted channels, monitoring for spread
mechanism: Not: A press conference — early volume maximizes reach, National media appearances to get ahead of it, Ignore it entirely; small claims always die on their own without any response
countermeasure: Match the response to the observed stage: a small, local claim is best met with local, proportionate correction while monitoring growth. Loud national response amplifies the claim; ignoring forfeits the window.

prompt: Name the move: "An ELA map shows bright patches across a photo's background. What is the correct reading?"
diagnosis: An indicator with innocent explanations that cannot by itself establish tampering
mechanism: Not: Proof that the background was digitally inserted in an editing program like Photoshop, Proof the image is a deepfake, A cryptographic attestation of the image's edits
countermeasure: ELA highlights areas of differing recompression response, which arise innocently from texture and saturation as well as from edits. It is an indicator that raises questions, never a verdict — exactly what the skill trains.

prompt: Name the move: "A photo has no C2PA manifest. What does that establish?"
diagnosis: Nothing about tampering — a missing manifest is not evidence of manipulation
mechanism: Not: The image was edited after capture, which is exactly why its manifest is missing, The image was generated by AI, The image's signature was stripped deliberately
countermeasure: Most cameras and tools still emit no manifest, so absence is the norm, not a red flag — the skill's core rule that missing provenance proves nothing about manipulation.

prompt: Name the move: "A viewer parses a photo's C2PA manifest successfully: it lists an editor application and a capture device. The viewer declares the image "verified authentic." What is the correct assessment?"
diagnosis: Wrong — parsing a manifest is not verifying it; signatures must validate
mechanism: Not: Right — a readable manifest is sufficient proof of the capture device listed, Right — editor presence proves only innocent edits, Wrong — C2PA manifests never cover edited images
countermeasure: The skill's central distinction: parsing a manifest only reads its claims; verification requires validating the cryptographic signatures across the credential chain. A readable manifest alone establishes nothing about authenticity.

prompt: Name the move: ""A headline reads: 'CORRUPT BUREAUCRATS SQUANDER BILLIONS ON SECRET ELITE PALACES' without citing a single budgetary line item or audit report.""
mechanism: Not: Glittering Generalities, Transfer Technique, Card Stacking
countermeasure: Using intense emotional valence and pejorative buzzwords to provoke visceral anger and bypass analytical scrutiny.

prompt: Name the move: ""If it is raining, the street is wet. The street is wet. Therefore, it is raining.""
mechanism: Not: Denying the Antecedent, Modus Ponens, Undistributed Middle
countermeasure: A formal deductive error: the street could be wet from a fire hydrant, street sweeper, or melting snow.

prompt: Name the move: ""The feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. Therefore, a feather cannot be dark.""
mechanism: Not: Amphiboly, Division Fallacy, Reification
countermeasure: Shifting between two distinct definitions of the word 'light' (weight vs illumination) within the same syllogism.

prompt: Name the move: ""A 2D Fourier Transform of a suspicious high-resolution headshot reveals a grid of high-frequency periodic spike artifacts across the power spectrum.""
mechanism: Not: Diffusion Noise Residual, Camera Bayer Demosaicing, CMOS Rolling Shutter Banding
countermeasure: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) using upsampling transposed convolutions leave characteristic periodic frequency grid spikes.

prompt: Name the move: ""After an election outcome is declared, 80% of poll commentators claim: 'I knew it was going to happen all along', despite their written forecasts stating the exact opposite 48 hours prior.""
mechanism: Not: Egocentric Bias, Actor-Observer Bias, Fundamental Attribution Error
countermeasure: The inclination to see events, after they have occurred, as having been predictable despite having had no basis for knowing.

prompt: Name the move: ""Every component of this supercomputer weighs less than 1 ounce. Therefore, the entire assembled supercomputer weighs less than 1 ounce.""
mechanism: Not: Fallacy of Division, Accident Fallacy, Ecological Fallacy
countermeasure: Erronously inferring that something is true of the whole from the fact that it is true of each individual part.

prompt: Name the move: ""The transport committee proposed a 15 km/h speed reduction outside primary schools. So they think cars are evil and want us all walking to work in the rain.""
mechanism: Not: Slippery Slope, False Dilemma, Hasty Generalisation
countermeasure: The actual proposal — a limited speed change near schools — is replaced by an absurd one that is easier to attack. This is not a slippery slope: no chain of consequences is claimed, the position itself has been swapped out.

prompt: Name the move: ""Either you support an immediate 100% military embargo on all trade with our neighboring rival, or you are a traitor who hates our homeland.""
mechanism: Not: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc, No True Scotsman, Begging the Question (Petitio Principii)
countermeasure: Artificially reduces a complex foreign policy spectrum to two extreme binaries while ignoring diplomatic nuances.

prompt: Name the move: ""That statistical method was developed by a mathematician who later joined a eugenics society, so any result produced with it is tainted.""
mechanism: Not: Ad Hominem (Circumstantial), Poisoning the Well, Guilt by Association
countermeasure: The objection is to the ORIGIN of the method, not to a person currently making an argument — that is what separates it from ad hominem. A technique's validity does not inherit its inventor's politics; that has to be shown mathematically.

prompt: Name the move: "Asked whether the audit found missing funds, the director replies: "What I will say is that this department has served this city for ninety years and our staff work incredibly hard.""
mechanism: Not: Straw Man, Appeal to Emotion, Begging the Question
countermeasure: The reply is true, warm, and about something else — the audit question is never engaged. It is not an appeal to emotion in the strict sense: no feeling is offered as EVIDENCE, the subject is simply changed.

prompt: Name the move: ""Both people I know who took that job quit within a year. It is clearly a terrible employer.""
mechanism: Not: Anecdotal Evidence, Fallacy of Composition, Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
countermeasure: A sample of two is generalised to an employer of unknown size. Anecdotal evidence is the close neighbour and would be the better answer if the anecdote were being used AGAINST statistics; here there are no statistics in play, only an over-broad leap.

prompt: Name the move: "An analyst reviews forty indicators, reports the three that moved together before the crash, and presents them as an early-warning signature."
mechanism: Not: Cherry Picking, Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc, Survivorship Bias
countermeasure: The pattern is drawn AFTER the data is seen — the target painted around the bullet holes. Cherry picking is the nearest miss: that would be selecting favourable data from a pre-existing claim, whereas here the claim itself is constructed from whichever indicators happened to align.

prompt: Name the move: ""A Nobel laureate in chemistry has said the new monetary policy will cause hyperinflation, so the case is settled.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Popularity, Ad Hominem, Appeal to Tradition (Argumentum ad Antiquitatem)
countermeasure: The credential is real but belongs to a different field. This is the harder version of the fallacy — the easy version cites someone with no expertise at all, while genuine authority misapplied is far more persuasive and far more common.

prompt: Name the move: ""This procedure has been standard practice in the guild for two hundred years. That is reason enough to keep it.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Authority, Appeal to Popularity, Begging the Question
countermeasure: Age is offered in place of evidence of effectiveness. Note that longevity is weak evidence rather than none — a practice that survived two centuries of use may work — but "it is old" is not the same claim as "it works", and only the second is being defended.

prompt: Name the move: ""The compound is plant-derived and completely natural, so it cannot be harmful in the doses we sell.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Ignorance, False Dilemma, Equivocation
countermeasure: Natural origin is treated as evidence of safety. Hemlock, asbestos and botulinum toxin are all natural; the property that matters is dose-response, which the claim quietly skips.

prompt: Name the move: ""No study has ever demonstrated that the additive is unsafe at these levels. Therefore it is safe.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to False Authority, Shifting the Burden of Proof, Hasty Generalisation
countermeasure: Absence of evidence of harm is converted into evidence of safety. Shifting the burden of proof is the near neighbour and is often bundled with it, but here nobody is being asked to disprove anything — the gap in the literature is itself being treated as a finding.

prompt: Name the move: ""Four million subscribers cannot be wrong about this trading strategy.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to False Authority (Ad Verecundiam), Astroturfing, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: Headcount is offered as proof. Astroturfing is the distractor worth pausing on: that would require the crowd to be MANUFACTURED, and nothing here suggests the subscribers are inauthentic — only that their number is irrelevant to whether the strategy works.

prompt: Name the move: ""If the server were compromised, outbound traffic would spike. Outbound traffic has spiked. So the server is compromised.""
mechanism: Not: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc, Hasty Generalisation, Circular Reasoning
countermeasure: The argument fails by its FORM: many other causes produce a traffic spike. Post hoc is the tempting alternative, but nothing here rests on the order of events — even if the spike came first, the inference would still be invalid.

prompt: Name the move: ""If the account were a bot, it would post at machine-regular intervals. It does not post at regular intervals. So it is not a bot.""
mechanism: Not: Affirming the Consequent (Formal Fallacy), Appeal to Ignorance, False Dilemma
countermeasure: Ruling out one signature does not rule out the category — modern automation deliberately jitters its timing. Distinguish it from affirming the consequent by which half is negated: here the IF-part is denied, there the THEN-part is affirmed.

prompt: Name the move: ""Every state-run outlet amplified the story. This outlet amplified the story. Therefore this outlet is state-run.""
mechanism: Not: Affirming the Consequent (Formal Fallacy), Guilt by Association, Hasty Generalisation
countermeasure: Sharing one property does not establish membership — plenty of independent outlets amplified it too. It is a syllogistic form error, close to affirming the consequent but stated over categories rather than conditionals.

prompt: Name the move: ""Either the footage is authentic or the timestamp was altered. The timestamp was altered. So the footage is not authentic.""
mechanism: Not: False Dilemma (Bifurcation), Denying the Antecedent (Formal Fallacy), Equivocation (Semantic Shift)
countermeasure: An inclusive "or" permits both to be true: real footage can carry a doctored timestamp. False dilemma is the close cousin — that would be an objection to the two options being the ONLY ones, whereas the error here is in what follows once one is affirmed.

prompt: Name the move: ""All verified accounts have a badge. This account has a badge. So it is verified." — the arguer insists the reasoning is fine because the conclusion happens to be true."
diagnosis: The form is invalid even though the conclusion is true
mechanism: Not: The argument is sound because the conclusion is true, The premises are false, which is the real problem, It is an informal fallacy of relevance
countermeasure: This is the point of the formal/informal distinction: validity is a property of STRUCTURE, not of outcome. A true conclusion reached by an invalid route gives you no reason to trust the route next time — which is exactly when it will mislead you.

prompt: Name the move: "A screening test flags 1 in 20 healthy people. A colleague reasons: "It flagged you, and it only flags 5% of healthy people, so there is a 95% chance you are ill.""
diagnosis: Base-Rate Neglect dressed as a formal inference
mechanism: Not: Affirming the Consequent (Formal Fallacy), Conjunction Fallacy, Appeal to False Authority
countermeasure: The false-positive RATE has been silently swapped for the probability of illness given a positive result. It looks like a formal move but the defect is in the content: without the prevalence of the disease, the conclusion cannot be computed at all.

prompt: Name the move: ""His argument commits a fallacy, so his conclusion is false.""
mechanism: Not: Ad Hominem, Circular Reasoning, Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam)
countermeasure: A bad argument for a claim leaves the claim exactly where it was — unsupported, not refuted. This is the failure mode a fallacy taxonomy itself invites, which is why it belongs in one.

prompt: Name the move: "An investigator convinced the fire was arson spends the afternoon interviewing neighbours who reported seeing someone near the building, and never contacts the electrician who serviced the panel that week."
mechanism: Not: Availability Heuristic, Anchoring Effect, Fundamental Attribution Error
countermeasure: The search itself is shaped by the hypothesis — disconfirming evidence is not rejected, it is never gathered. That selective-search step is what separates it from the availability heuristic, where evidence comes to mind unbidden rather than being sought out.

prompt: Name the move: "Two readers are shown the same ambiguous polling table. Each reports that it supports the candidate they already preferred, and each can point to a column that does."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Anchoring Effect, False Balance (Bothsidesism)
countermeasure: Both readers see all the data, so the bias is in INTERPRETATION rather than in what was collected — which predicts that shared evidence drives people apart rather than together. Plain confirmation bias is the broader family; this is the specific mechanism operating here.

prompt: Name the move: "A trader keeps a journal of every prediction that came true and remembers the losing calls as "the market being irrational that week"."
mechanism: Not: Hindsight Bias, Sunk Cost Fallacy, Survivorship Bias
countermeasure: The record and the memory are curated after the fact. Hindsight bias is the neighbour — that would be misremembering how confident he WAS beforehand, whereas here the question is which events he retains at all.

prompt: Name the move: "Asked to discover the rule behind the sequence 2-4-6, a participant proposes 8-10-12, then 20-22-24, then 100-102-104, and concludes the rule is "add two"."
mechanism: Not: Hasty Generalisation (Secundum Quid), Anchoring Effect, Conjunction Fallacy
countermeasure: Every probe is one the hypothesis predicts will succeed, so none could have falsified it. Hasty generalisation concerns too little evidence; the defect here is that no quantity of this KIND of evidence would help — the participant never tried 1-2-3.

prompt: Name the move: "A team reviewing a failed launch reads the pre-launch risk memo and finds that it "obviously flagged the problem", though at the time nobody acted on it."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Selective Recall, Fundamental Attribution Error / Ingroup Favoritism
countermeasure: Knowing the outcome makes the warning legible in a way it was not beforehand. This is why post-incident reviews asking "who missed this" produce worse findings than ones asking "what was visible at the time".

prompt: Name the move: "A researcher pre-registers a hypothesis, collects the data, finds nothing, then reports a subgroup where the effect appears and describes it as the analysis she had planned."
mechanism: Not: Texas Sharpshooter, Selective Recall, Confirmation Bias
countermeasure: The move is presenting a post-hoc hypothesis as a pre-hoc one, which destroys the statistical guarantee the pre-registration existed to provide. Texas sharpshooter names the same shape informally; HARKing is what it is called inside a research protocol.

prompt: Name the move: "After a week of coverage of a shark attack, beach visitors rate swimming as more dangerous than the drive to the coast."
mechanism: Not: Anchoring Effect, Confirmation Bias, Base-Rate Neglect (Prior Insensitivity)
countermeasure: Ease of recall stands in for frequency, and coverage drives recall. Base-rate neglect is arguably also present, but the ENGINE is vividness and repetition — which is precisely what makes this exploitable by whoever controls the volume.

prompt: Name the move: "Asked whether more English words begin with R or have R as their third letter, most people answer "begin with R". The opposite is true."
mechanism: Not: Anchoring Effect, Conjunction Fallacy (Linda Problem), Confirmation Bias
countermeasure: Words are indexed in memory by first letter, so first-letter examples are retrievable and third-letter ones are not. The judgement tracks the accessibility of examples rather than their number — a clean case, since no emotion or media coverage is involved.

prompt: Name the move: "A security team fresh from reviewing a phishing breach puts most of next quarter into email filtering, while an unpatched external service goes unfunded."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Sunk Cost Fallacy (Escalation of Commitment), Anchoring Effect
countermeasure: The most recent and most discussed threat crowds out the assessed one. It is not sunk cost — no prior investment is being defended; the distortion is that recency has been mistaken for risk.

prompt: Name the move: "A local paper runs six stories in a month about assaults in one park. Reported crime there does not change, but residents petition to close it."
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing, Hasty Generalisation, Loaded / Emotive Language
countermeasure: The frequency of COVERAGE changed, not the frequency of events, and the two are being read as one signal. Note that this requires no bad actor at all — ordinary editorial choices produce it.

prompt: Name the move: "A drug described as having "90% survival" is accepted far more readily than the same drug described as having "10% mortality"."
mechanism: Not: Availability Heuristic, Anchoring Effect, Equivocation (Semantic Shift)
countermeasure: The numbers are identical, so nothing about the evidence changed — only which outcome the wording makes easy to picture. It sits beside availability rather than inside it: availability concerns what comes to mind, framing what the phrasing puts there.

prompt: Name the move: "An executive says air travel has become far more dangerous, citing three crashes she can name from the past year — none of which she could have named a year ago."
mechanism: Not: Hasty Generalisation (Secundum Quid), Confirmation Bias, Survivorship Bias
countermeasure: That she can now name them is the whole of the evidence, and namability grew because coverage did. Hasty generalisation tempts, but the flaw is not sample SIZE — it is that the sample is drawn from memory, which is not a random sampler.

prompt: Name the move: "A negotiator opens with a figure far above any plausible settlement. The final agreement lands well above what either side privately expected."
mechanism: Not: Framing Effect, Sunk Cost Fallacy, Appeal to Authority
countermeasure: The opening number does not need to be credible to work; it only needs to be first. Framing is the neighbour — that would require the same value described differently, whereas here a single irrelevant number drags the whole scale.

prompt: Name the move: "Asked "was the population above or below 20 million?" and then to estimate it, respondents guess far higher than a group asked "above or below 2 million?" first."
mechanism: Not: Availability Heuristic, Confirmation Bias, Conjunction Fallacy
countermeasure: The comparison figure carries no information about the answer, yet it sets the range people adjust within — and adjustment is reliably insufficient. This is the cleanest demonstration precisely because the anchor is transparently arbitrary.

prompt: Name the move: "A headline reads "Department seeks $4bn — critics say $3.2bn is enough". Later coverage debates the gap. The prior year's budget was $900m."
mechanism: Not: False Balance (Bothsidesism), Loaded / Emotive Language, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: Both published figures sit far above the historical baseline, so the "sceptical" number still anchors the debate high. False balance is a real distractor here, but the two positions are not being presented as equally supported — the distortion is in the numeric range they jointly establish.

prompt: Name the move: "A menu lists a $180 tasting option at the top. Sales of the $95 option rise sharply, although it did not change."
mechanism: Not: Framing Effect, Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon), Appeal to Nature
countermeasure: The expensive item may sell rarely and still earn its place by re-scaling every other price. Nothing about the $95 dish changed — only the reference point it is judged against.

prompt: Name the move: "An analyst's first estimate of a breach at 40,000 records is later shown to be far too low, but every subsequent revision lands between 45,000 and 60,000. The eventual figure is 2.1 million."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Availability Heuristic, Hindsight Bias (Knew-It-All-Along Effect)
countermeasure: Revisions crawl away from the initial figure instead of being re-derived from scratch. Confirmation bias is close, but the analyst is not defending a conclusion — she is updating, just far too slowly and always from the same starting point.

prompt: Name the move: "A survey asks "how much would you pay to avoid this outcome, given others paid around $50?" before recording the respondent's own figure."
mechanism: Not: Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon), Framing Effect, Astroturfing
countermeasure: The reference is doing two jobs — social proof and numeric anchor — but the measurable distortion is the numeric one, which appears even when respondents are told the figure was randomly generated. Bandwagon would require the crowd itself to be the reason offered.

prompt: Name the move: "A driver cut off in traffic mutters "what a selfish idiot". When he does the same thing an hour later, it is because he is late for a hospital appointment."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Hindsight Bias, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: Others' behaviour is explained by character, one's own by circumstance. The asymmetry is the diagnostic feature — either explanation alone could be reasonable; holding both at once is not.

prompt: Name the move: "When our side's official misstates a figure it is "a briefing error under pressure". When theirs does, it is "a deliberate attempt to mislead the public"."
mechanism: Not: Fundamental Attribution Error / Ingroup Favoritism, Loaded / Emotive Language, Whataboutism (Tu Quoque)
countermeasure: The same act receives a situational reading for the in-group and a dispositional one for the out-group. The general attribution error is the parent category; naming the in-group/out-group split matters because it is what makes the bias politically load-bearing.

prompt: Name the move: "A manager reads a team's missed deadline as a motivation problem, without checking that the upstream dependency shipped three weeks late."
mechanism: Not: Confirmation Bias, Base-Rate Neglect, Hindsight Bias
countermeasure: Dispositional explanation is reached for first, and the situational one is never tested. Confirmation bias would require a prior hypothesis being defended; here the leap to character happens before any hypothesis exists.

prompt: Name the move: "A profile explains a founder's success entirely through her discipline and vision, mentioning in passing that the family funded the first two years."
mechanism: Not: Survivorship Bias, Availability Heuristic (Ease of Recall), Appeal to Authority
countermeasure: Traits are credited with an outcome that had substantial situational support. Survivorship bias is the tempting alternative and would apply to a claim about founders in general; this is about the causal account of one case.

prompt: Name the move: "A commentator argues that because a hostile state benefits from a protest movement, the protesters must be acting on its instructions."
mechanism: Not: Guilt by Association, Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc, Astroturfing
countermeasure: Benefit is treated as evidence of authorship. Astroturfing is the sharp distractor: that is a real phenomenon and would need evidence of coordination — account clustering, funding, synchronised messaging — none of which "someone benefits" supplies.

prompt: Name the move: ""Linda is 31, single, outspoken, and deeply concerned with social justice. Which is more probable: (A) Linda is a bank teller, or (B) Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement?""
mechanism: Not: Base Rate Neglect, Availability Cascade, Hindsight Bias
countermeasure: The probability of two events occurring together (A and B) cannot exceed the probability of either event occurring individually (A).

prompt: Name the move: "A reviewer marks a colleague's error as carelessness and their own identical error, found the next day, as a symptom of an unclear spec."
mechanism: Not: Fundamental Attribution Error / Ingroup Favoritism, Selective Recall, Hindsight Bias
countermeasure: The precise form is the SELF versus other split, rather than in-group versus out-group. Both are attribution errors; distinguishing them matters because they have different remedies — one is fixed by perspective-taking, the other by rules applied before you know whose work it is.

prompt: Name the move: "After an outage, the report concludes "human error by the on-call engineer" and closes. The runbook had been wrong since March."
mechanism: Not: Hindsight Bias, Confirmation Bias, Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam)
countermeasure: Attributing the failure to a person ends the investigation exactly where the systemic cause begins. Hindsight bias is likely present too, but the load-bearing error is locating the cause in a character rather than in the conditions.

prompt: Name the move: ""She is quiet, reads constantly, and loves order. Is she more likely to be a librarian, or a librarian who plays in a band?""
mechanism: Not: Base-Rate Neglect, Representativeness Heuristic, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: A conjunction can never be more probable than either of its parts, however well the extra detail fits the picture. Representativeness is the MECHANISM that produces the error; the conjunction violation is the error itself, which is what the question asks for.

prompt: Name the move: "A test is 99% accurate for a condition affecting 1 in 10,000 people. A positive result comes back. A colleague says "so it is 99% certain"."
mechanism: Not: Conjunction Fallacy, Anchoring Effect, Appeal to False Authority
countermeasure: With that prevalence, the great majority of positives are false positives — roughly 1% of the healthy 9,999 outnumbers the single true case. The test's accuracy is real; the mistake is using it without the prior.

prompt: Name the move: ""Red has come up six times in a row, so black is due.""
mechanism: Not: Base-Rate Neglect, Hindsight Bias, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: Independent trials have no memory. Note the mirror-image error is equally common — concluding that red is "hot" and will continue — and both come from expecting short runs to look like long-run averages.

prompt: Name the move: "A programme is judged effective because the schools that adopted it improved. Schools that adopted it and closed before the follow-up were not counted."
mechanism: Not: Selective Recall, Base-Rate Neglect, Texas Sharpshooter
countermeasure: The sample is defined by having survived to be measured, so the failures are structurally invisible. Cherry picking would require someone choosing which data to show; here nobody chose — the selection is done by the measurement itself, which makes it much harder to notice.

prompt: Name the move: "Four hundred accounts supporting a zoning proposal were created within the same eleven-day window last year, and share a posting-time distribution unlike the platform baseline."
mechanism: Not: Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon), Brigading, Availability Heuristic
countermeasure: Creation-date clustering plus an anomalous activity rhythm is coordination evidence, which is what separates this from bandwagon — bandwagon is a fallacy about crowd size being offered as a reason, astroturfing is a claim that the crowd is manufactured.

prompt: Name the move: "A "grassroots parents' coalition" launches with a professional website, a media kit, and a registered agent shared with an industry trade body."
mechanism: Not: Appeal to False Authority, False Balance (Bothsidesism), Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour
countermeasure: The tell is infrastructure appearing before membership — real grassroots groups accumulate capability slowly and messily. The shared registered agent is the documentary link that turns a suspicion into a finding.

prompt: Name the move: "Two hundred reviews of a contested documentary use the phrase "finally someone said it" within a six-hour window, across accounts with no other overlap."
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing (Manufactured Grassroots), Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon), Availability Cascade
countermeasure: Near-identical phrasing in a tight window is the signature; the accounts need not be fake for the BEHAVIOUR to be coordinated, which is why this term is preferred to astroturfing when authorship is unproven. Choosing the stronger label without evidence of manufacture is itself an over-read.

prompt: Name the move: "In a ninety-second answer, a speaker makes nineteen separate factual assertions, four of which are false and none of which the opponent has time to address."
mechanism: Not: Red Herring, Straw Man, Whataboutism (Tu Quoque)
countermeasure: The asymmetry between assertion cost and refutation cost is the weapon; the individual claims barely matter. A red herring diverts to ONE other topic, which is a different and much cheaper attack to answer.

prompt: Name the move: ""When confronted about human rights abuses in prison facilities, the minister replies: 'What about your country's mass surveillance programs in 2013?'""
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing (Manufactured Grassroots), Gish Gallop, Gaslighting
countermeasure: Deflects criticism by raising a counter-accusation of hypocrisy without addressing the underlying offense.

prompt: Name the move: "After a leak, a network publishes six mutually incompatible explanations within a day, none pushed harder than the others."
mechanism: Not: Gish Gallop, False Balance (Bothsidesism), Appeal to Ignorance
countermeasure: The goal is not to be believed but to make belief feel arbitrary — mutual incompatibility is a feature, since a consistent lie could be refuted. A Gish gallop tries to WIN an exchange; this tries to exhaust the possibility of one.

prompt: Name the move: "A records request is answered with 40,000 unsorted, unsearchable scanned pages within the statutory deadline."
mechanism: Not: Gish Gallop, Red Herring, Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam)
countermeasure: The request is technically satisfied while the answer is made unreachable. It shares its mechanism with the Gish gallop — cost asymmetry — but happens in a procedural rather than rhetorical setting, which is why it is rarely recognised as the same move.

prompt: Name the move: "A moderator's queue receives 12,000 near-duplicate reports against one account in an hour, each individually plausible."
mechanism: Not: Astroturfing, Gish Gallop, Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour
countermeasure: Volume is aimed at a process rather than at an audience — the target is the moderation system's capacity. It overlaps with coordinated inauthentic behaviour, but brigading can be entirely authentic people acting together, which is what makes it hard to police.

prompt: Name the move: "A segment on a well-replicated finding gives equal airtime to the one researcher who disputes it and to the consensus position, without saying how many hold each."
mechanism: Not: Appeal to False Authority, Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon), Manufactured Doubt
countermeasure: Equal time misrepresents the state of the evidence as an even split. Manufactured doubt is the strategy this often serves, but that names a deliberate campaign; false balance is the editorial artefact, which frequently occurs without one.

prompt: Name the move: "Internal documents show an industry planned to "establish doubt as the product" rather than to win the scientific argument outright."
mechanism: Not: False Balance (Bothsidesism), Appeal to Ignorance, Firehose of Falsehood
countermeasure: The objective is uncertainty itself, because inaction follows from it — no positive counter-claim needs to survive scrutiny. False balance is the media surface this strategy exploits, not the strategy.

prompt: Name the move: "A debate on whether a bridge is structurally sound is staged between a structural engineer and a local columnist, introduced as "two views"."
mechanism: Not: Appeal to False Authority (Ad Verecundiam), Red Herring, Ad Hominem
countermeasure: The pairing implies comparable standing on a question where it does not exist. Appeal to false authority is the near miss and would apply if the COLUMNIST'S credentials were being cited as support; here the fallacy is committed by the framing, not by either speaker.

prompt: Name the move: "An article reports "scientists are divided" and cites two studies for and two against, from a literature containing several hundred."
mechanism: Not: Cherry Picking, Hasty Generalisation, Availability Heuristic (Ease of Recall)
countermeasure: A 2-to-2 presentation of a lopsided literature manufactures a division. Cherry picking is genuinely also present, which is worth noticing: false balance is usually implemented THROUGH selective citation rather than being an alternative to it.

prompt: Name the move: "A broadcaster defends the pairing: "We do not take sides. We present both positions and let the audience decide.""
diagnosis: Neutrality as an evasion of editorial judgement
mechanism: Not: False Balance (Bothsidesism), Appeal to Ignorance, Argumentum ad Populum (Bandwagon)
countermeasure: Deciding what counts as a "position" worth airing is already an editorial judgement; declining to weigh evidence does not avoid influence, it just hides where the influence was applied. This is the defence that keeps false balance in place, which is why it is worth being able to name separately.

prompt: Name the move: "A journalist notes that on a question where evidence is genuinely unsettled, she gave both hypotheses equal weight and said so explicitly."
diagnosis: This is appropriate — balance matches the actual state of evidence
mechanism: Not: False Balance (Bothsidesism), Manufactured Doubt, Appeal to Ignorance
countermeasure: False balance is not "presenting two sides", it is presenting them as more equal than the evidence warrants. When the evidence really is split, equal treatment is accurate — and an operator who has learned to shout "false balance" at every two-sided piece has acquired a reflex, not a skill.

prompt: Name the move: "A regulator's summary lists "arguments for" and "arguments against" in parallel columns of equal length, omitting that one column's entries were each rebutted in the evidence sessions."
mechanism: Not: Cherry Picking, Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam), Straw Man
countermeasure: Symmetrical presentation carries an implicit claim about symmetrical strength, and the rebuttals were the load-bearing information. Layout is an argument, even when no sentence in the document makes one.

prompt: Name the move: ""In a 10-minute televised debate, a candidate unleashes 47 distinct, rapid-fire half-truths and fabricated statistics, making real-time refutation impossible in the remaining time.""

countermeasure: Overwhelming an opponent with an excessive volume of specious arguments that take far longer to disprove than to utter.

prompt: Name the move: "One outlet reports "the council seized the land"; another reports "the council acquired the land". The legal process described is identical."
mechanism: Not: Framing Effect, Equivocation (Semantic Shift), Straw Man
countermeasure: The verb imports a verdict before any argument is made. It differs from equivocation in that no term shifts meaning WITHIN an argument — the word choice smuggles the conclusion in at the start.

prompt: Name the move: "A policy brief refers throughout to "the flood of arrivals" and "communities under strain", without citing a figure."
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Fear, Hasty Generalisation, Availability Heuristic (Ease of Recall)
countermeasure: Metaphor does the work of evidence: "flood" implies volume, threat and lack of agency simultaneously. Appeal to fear is the neighbour — that names an explicit frightening consequence, whereas here the fear is carried by vocabulary alone.

prompt: Name the move: "A question in a survey reads: "Do you support the failed and wasteful subsidy programme?""
mechanism: Not: Loaded / Emotive Language, False Dilemma (Bifurcation), Begging the Question (Petitio Principii)
countermeasure: Both answers concede that the programme failed and was wasteful — the presupposition is unanswerable within the question. Loaded language is present too, but the structural defect is that there is no response that does not accept the premise.

prompt: Name the move: "A campaign describes its own supporters as "concerned citizens" and its opponents' identical activity as "agitators bussed in from outside"."
mechanism: Not: Ingroup Attribution Asymmetry, Astroturfing, Whataboutism (Tu Quoque)
countermeasure: The same behaviour receives opposite labels. There is an attribution asymmetry underneath, which makes that a defensible second choice — but what is being asked about is the vocabulary doing the work, and the question is which lever is being pulled on the reader.

prompt: Name the move: ""The report says the risk is not significant. So there is no meaningful risk to residents.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam), Hasty Generalisation, Straw Man
countermeasure: "Significant" moves from its statistical sense to its everyday one between the two sentences. A statistically non-significant result can describe a large and worrying effect measured imprecisely — the terms are not interchangeable, which is exactly what the argument relies on.

prompt: Name the move: ""Every socialist regime has collapsed." Shown a counterexample: "That one was not truly socialist.""
mechanism: Not: Equivocation (Semantic Shift), Circular Reasoning, Begging the Question
countermeasure: The category is redefined mid-argument so the claim cannot be tested. It is a specific form of semantic shift, and worth distinguishing: ordinary equivocation exploits an existing ambiguity, while this one MANUFACTURES the ambiguity in response to evidence.

prompt: Name the move: ""The data is anonymised — no names are stored. So the dataset cannot identify anyone.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Ignorance, Hasty Generalisation, Affirming the Consequent (Formal Fallacy)
countermeasure: "Anonymised" is used first in the narrow sense of name removal and then in the strong sense of non-identifiability, which are famously not the same — postcode, birth date and sex re-identify most people. The word is doing two different jobs in two consecutive clauses.

prompt: Name the move: ""Of course the theory is only a theory — so it is hardly established fact.""
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam), Straw Man, False Dilemma (Bifurcation)
countermeasure: The technical sense of "theory" — an explanatory framework supported by evidence — is swapped for the colloquial "guess". Note that the sentence contains no false statement, which is why equivocation is so much harder to answer than a lie.

prompt: Name the move: "A spokesperson: "We have never had a data breach." Later: incidents were logged as "security events" under an internal policy that reserves "breach" for confirmed exfiltration."
mechanism: Not: Appeal to Ignorance (Argumentum ad Ignorantiam), No True Scotsman, Loaded / Emotive Language
countermeasure: A private definition is used to make a public claim that a listener will read under the ordinary definition. It is close to No True Scotsman, but nothing is being redefined in RESPONSE to a counterexample — the narrow definition was established in advance, which makes it more deliberate rather than less.

prompt: Name the move: ""Free speech means I can say what I like. So a platform removing my post is a free speech violation.""

countermeasure: The phrase shifts from a moral principle to a specific legal constraint on government action, and the conclusion only follows under the second reading while the premise is only plausible under the first.
